doc.title: Laurena Diggs and Carrie Boote Interview, 1959-05-25

title: Organ grinders, amateur nights and learning to perform without teachers
summary: She had no voice teacher; she describes street music, amateur nights, Clarence Williams, and self-taught dancing.

story.theme_name: Medicine shows, minstrels, circuses and the black theater circuit
story.community_name: On the road with minstrel, carnival and tent shows

blocks.x: I'm sort of jumping around today, but, uh, you say you had piano teachers? Did you have a voice teacher, too?

Me? No, no. Just, what little I tried was just something I, you know. Mm-hm. they used to have organ grinders, you know, going around the street and you put the nickel and the man would play your piece. Well, most children save their nickels, you know, and when he'd come around, they'd get out there and dance up a breeze right on the street, you know. And there are so many children and so many people here. Years ago, if you wanted a piano player, you didn't have to go look all around. You could look out and see most anybody could hit a tune and didn't know a word of music. Now, just like this Steve Lewis, I don't think he knew music and he played all down, I don't know what this, some white club, West End, isn't it West End here? Well, he played down there in the ten of the years and he didn't know anything about reading music, but he could play anything you asked him to, see. Well, now, during that time, that man would play the organ. Sometimes they had a monkey, you know, would go around and pick up the things and the kids would get out on the sidewalk and just like the dance, you know, behind the band and have fun dancing out in the street. Well, that was when I was small, you know. And then they used to have amateur night. Clarence Williams and Edith Taylor, I think that's his wife, they used to have amateur nights. They had a show round up in here. I don't know where it is. Where was it? Where Prince Goodwood Hospital is. Yeah, I forgot. But you see, you would get on this amateur, you know, and a lot of people just would take up from singing and dancing out in the street. And then if they think they got good, they'd get on amateur night and you'd dance there. You may have went on a week engagement at the Regal or something like that. And a lot of people just went on from that. And just late years, people really worried about voice culture and theatrical. Well, in the early 20s, you just went on and got up there and sing. And went on dancing. They didn't call it tap dancing. They called it buck dancing, you know. And you could just get out there and cut a step and look like, just like in a course, they had somebody to show you the step all right. But if you didn't have eye enough to just catch on, you was lost. Nobody taking time, you know. They had someone to train you. But in the meantime, you caught on. You should know something about it without a teacher. So when any time you went to this, worked in a nightclub, you'd stand there and look a while and fall in line. And you'd start stumbling off with something. And it went right along. Because I know some of the leading, just like Ethel Waters. Ethel Waters, she worked in a street fair with a fellow named James Seymour. It used to be Jeanette and Seymour. They were a very popular team. And Neoma Brown and McGraw. You heard of Brown and McGraw?
